    Frequently asked questions

    The first step is identifying your production goals—what products you want to make (milk, cheese, yogurt, butter, etc.)—and estimating your daily milk intake. This helps determine the type and size of equipment needed.

    Yes. Dairy processing facilities must meet local health, safety, and food regulation standards. You’ll need permits, inspections, and certifications before you can operate legally.

    Before setting up your dairy processing line, it's essential to decide which products you want to make—such as fluid milk, yogurt, cheese, butter, or cream. Each product has unique processing requirements, equipment, and regulatory considerations. Defining your product lineup early ensures you invest in the right machinery and facility layout from the start.

    Selecting the right packaging material depends on the type of dairy product you’re processing. For example:

    • Milk is commonly packed in plastic bottles, cartons, or glass bottles.

    • Yogurt is often packaged in plastic cups or tubs with foil lids.

    • Cheese may require vacuum-sealed plastic pouches or wax-coated wraps.

    • Butter is typically wrapped in foil, parchment, or placed in tubs.


    The packaging must protect the product, preserve freshness, and comply with food safety regulations. It also plays a key role in branding and shelf appeal.

    Once you've selected your products and packaging, the next step is identifying the equipment needed for production. Common dairy processing equipment includes:


    • Milk reception tanks for raw milk intake

    • Pasteurizers (batch or HTST) for heat treatment

    • Homogenizers (optional) for consistent texture

    • Fermentation tanks for yogurt or cultured products

    • Butter churns for cream-to-butter conversion

    • Cheese vats and molds for cheese production

    • Filling and packaging machines tailored to your product type

    • CIP systems for automated cleaning


    Equipment should meet food-grade standards (like 3A Sanitary) and be sized according to your production volume.

    This depends on your production volume and type of products. Small-scale setups can start in spaces as small as 500–1000 sq. ft., while larger facilities require significantly more room for equipment, cold storage, and packaging areas.

    Absolutely. Many dairy startups begin with small-scale batch equipment and grow into larger operations as demand increases. Modular equipment helps make scaling easier.

    Depending on the scale and complexity, it can take from 2 to 6 months, including planning, ordering equipment, installation, and getting regulatory approvals.
